answer.rationale: Only one move this cycle; the primary supply contract expires in 14 days, the incumbent has refused to reopen price, finance requires an 18% cut, and the line is running at 94% with no buffer — so a full switch-and-hope would breach delivery risk. memory_c4 says renegotiation recovered margin when the incumbent moved on both price and payment terms, but it does not say the incumbent held firm in a tight cycle; with this incumbent explicitly refusing to reopen price, the lever from c4 is closed here. memory_c2 documents a prior low-cost primary swap that cut unit cost sharply, onboarded quickly, and kept invoicing accurate — that is the strongest evidence in the inherited record for hitting finance's 18% cut without adding risk. memory_c1 warns that incumbent renewal preserved integration stability across two cycles with no migration work, which is the reason a same-cycle full swap is too aggressive when the line is at 94%. Plan: award a small, bounded share of primary volume to the low-cost vendor on a short evaluation track — enough to realize the unit-cost savings cited in c2, with a service-level and integration gate before scaling — and use the lever c4 documents (benchmarking, payment terms) at the next renewal to move the incumbent on the remaining share. This single move targets minimum TCO without inflating delivery risk on a 94%-utilization, no-buffer line.
